nameStory: The pygmy sperm whale gets its name from being the smallest member of the sperm whale family, earning the 'pygmy' designation despite still being quite large by most standards. Like its giant cousin the sperm whale, it has a rounded, oil-filled head called a spermaceti organ that early whalers mistook for sperm. The name stuck even after scientists realized the waxy substance was actually used for echolocation and buoyancy control.
description: The pygmy sperm whale is a mysterious, rarely-seen marine mammal that looks quite different from the classic whale shape most people imagine. It has a distinctive squared-off head with a small, underslung jaw that gives it an almost shark-like profile. These compact whales reach about 11 feet long and weigh up to 900 pounds, making them much smaller than their famous sperm whale relatives. Most of what we know about them comes from individuals that have washed ashore, as they're incredibly elusive in the wild.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Compact whale about the size of a large dolphin, with a distinctively squared-off, blunt head that looks almost chopped off at the front

idTips.label: Head Features
idTips.description: Small, narrow underslung jaw positioned well back from the front of the head, creating a shark-like profile when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Dark bluish-gray to black on top, fading to lighter gray or pinkish-white on the belly, with skin that appears smooth and rubbery

idTips.label: Dorsal Fin
idTips.description: Small, curved dorsal fin positioned far back on the body, much farther back than most dolphins or porpoises

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Extremely shy and elusive, typically floating motionless at the surface or diving immediately when disturbed, unlike the playful behavior of dolphins

habitat: Pygmy sperm whales prefer deep ocean waters off the continental shelf, typically found in areas over 600 feet deep. In New England waters, they're most likely encountered in the deep waters beyond the continental shelf break, particularly in the Gulf of Maine's deeper basins. They favor temperate to tropical waters and are rarely seen close to shore except when stranded.

seasonality.spring: Most strandings in New England occur during spring months, possibly related to changes in ocean currents and prey distribution as waters warm.
seasonality.summer: May be present in deeper offshore waters during summer, but sightings are extremely rare due to their elusive nature and preference for deep ocean habitats.
seasonality.fall: Some evidence suggests they may move to deeper waters during fall months, making encounters even less likely than usual.
seasonality.winter: Likely move to warmer southern waters during winter months, with virtually no records from New England waters during this season.

funFact: When threatened, pygmy sperm whales can release a cloud of reddish-brown intestinal fluid that acts like squid ink, creating a murky screen that lets them escape from predators - they're the only whales known to use this ninja-like defense strategy!
confusionNotes: Stranded pygmy sperm whales are sometimes mistaken for small pilot whales or large dolphins, but the pygmy's distinctively squared-off head and tiny underslung jaw are unique. Remember: if the head looks like it was cut off with a cleaver and the jaw seems too small for the head, you're likely looking at a pygmy sperm whale.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'pygmy,' these whales are still quite large compared to dolphins and porpoises - the name only makes sense when comparing them to their massive sperm whale cousins that can reach 60 feet long. The extreme rarity of sightings (only 2 recorded observations in New England) means most people will only encounter them as stranded individuals on beaches.
compareHints: The pygmy sperm whale is the only member of its genus found in New England waters, but it can be compared to the dwarf sperm whale found in warmer waters further south. Pygmy sperm whales are larger and have their small dorsal fin positioned further back on their body. Unlike true sperm whales, pygmies have a much more compact body and lack the distinctive sloped forehead of their giant relatives.
